w: What's tested Dr. Herr's study guide for this lecture: disorders of testicular development and descent (cryptorchidism), the major categories of testicular tumors (germ cell tumors, 95 percent, against the sex cord-stromal tumors; seminoma against the non-seminomatous tumors), the common infections of the male reproductive tract, and the major benign and malignant prostate disorders (BPH, prostatic adenocarcinoma and its Gleason grading) Her two closing reminders: "cryptorchidism is a predisposing factor to testicular cancer," and phimosis is a predisposing factor to carcinoma of the penis HPV in the male genital tract: condyloma acuminatum is benign, from the low-risk types 6 and 11; penile intraepithelial neoplasia comes from the high-risk types 16 and 18 ("the lower numbers, 6 and 11, are benign; higher numbers, 16 and 18, are premalignant"), or, in older men, without HPV, from lichen sclerosus The prostate's zones predict its disease: BPH around the urethra, which obstructs the urine; carcinoma in the peripheral zone, which spreads to bone and makes it (osteoblastic), with PSA in the blood The bladder: the urothelium, the benign conditions (congenital anomalies, reflux, diverticula, stones, cystitis), and urothelial carcinoma: 90 percent of urinary tract tumors, most of them in the bladder, with smoking the strongest risk factor What the lecture said you don't need: the WHO classifications of urinary tract and testicular tumors, the two molecular pathways of urothelial carcinoma, retroperitoneal fibrosis, the seminoma's look under the microscope, and the details of each non-seminomatous tumor ("you just need to know seminomatous versus non-seminomatous") 1 Cryptorchidism, a testis hidden outside the scrotum: the testes descend from the retroperitoneum through the inguinal canal; body heat halts spermatogenesis, so infertility and testicular cancer; surgery if it hasn't come down by the second year prevents the infertility, but the cancer risk stays Study guide + recording · 6 questions in the bank Know this Cryptorchidism: an undescended testis at body temperature can't make sperm. Wait up to the second year, then surgery; surgery prevents the infertility, but the testicular cancer risk stays. "Crypto means hidden": in cryptorchidism a testis is hidden, not in the scrotum. The testes develop retroperitoneally and descend through the inguinal canal into the scrotum before birth; the lecture said about 1 in 10 newborns have at least one undescended testis. The clinician waits through the first year, up to the second, for it to come down; if it hasn't come down by about 2 years old, it needs surgery. Why: the retroperitoneum and the inguinal canal are at body temperature, 37 °C, and that heat halts spermatogenesis, leading to infertility and testicular cancer. Correcting it surgically prevents the infertility, but "the risk of testicular cancer is still a possibility for that kid." The closing reminder: cryptorchidism is a predisposing factor to testicular cancer. 2 The categories of testicular tumors: 95 percent are germ cell tumors, from the spermatogonia, cured in more than 95 percent; the rest are sex cord-stromal tumors (Sertoli and Leydig cells) or mixed, with lymphoma (secondary) and metastases in older men Study guide + recording · 6 questions in the bank Know this From Dr. Herr's study guide, for Dr. Dal Zotto's lecture. Know cryptorchidism (why the testis has to come down: body heat halts spermatogenesis, so infertility and testicular cancer, and surgery leaves the cancer risk), the categories of testicular tumors (95 percent germ cell tumors, the rest mostly sex cord-stromal; seminoma versus non-seminomatous), the infections (syphilis, gonorrhea and chlamydia of the glans and foreskin; gonorrhea and chlamydia in epididymitis; orchitis uncommon), and the prostate: BPH around the urethra against adenocarcinoma in the peripheral zone, with PSA, osteoblastic bone metastases and Gleason grading. 95 percent germ cell tumors, from the spermatogonia; the rest sex cord-stromal (Sertoli, Leydig) or mixed, plus lymphoma (secondary) and metastases in older men. Germ cell tumors are cured in more than 95 percent. 95 percent of testicular tumors are germ cell tumors, from the spermatogonia. The rest are sex cord-stromal tumors (from the Sertoli and Leydig cells) or mixed tumors, and in older men, lymphoma (involving the testis secondarily, not starting there) and metastases. The incidence differs from country to country and, unlike penile cancer, isn't tied to low socioeconomic status; no one knows the factors. Norway has the highest incidence, and Hispanic men have a high incidence too. Germ cell tumors are cured in more than 95 percent of cases, so in general they behave well. The risk factor to know is cryptorchidism. 3 Seminoma versus the non-seminomatous germ cell tumors: seminoma is the most frequent, in young adults, white and solid without hemorrhage or necrosis, tied to cryptorchidism, usually without a serum marker, and radiosensitive; embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma and teratoma are more aggressive and don't respond as well Study guide + recording · 5 questions in the bank Know this Seminoma: the most frequent, young adults in their 30s and 40s, white, multinodular and solid with no hemorrhage or necrosis, tied to cryptorchidism, usually no serum marker (the pathologist diagnoses it). Seminoma, the most frequent: white, multinodular and solid, with no hemorrhage and no necrosis. A tumor of young adults, in their 30s and 40s ("if I see a young adult with a testicular tumor, I'm going to think, okay, this has a high chance to be a seminoma"). It is associated with cryptorchidism and usually has no serum tumor marker the clinician can measure, so it needs a pathologist to make the diagnosis. Non-seminomatous tumors: a germ cell can give rise to any tissue in the body, so these recapitulate the tissues of fetal life: embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma and teratoma. They are more aggressive than seminoma, and choriocarcinoma most of all. Hyperplasia of both the glands and the stroma of the prostate, around the urethra, so it obstructs the urethra and the flow of urine. It is very common: "Guys, you are going to have it. You cannot avoid this. After 50s, your prostate is going to start to be hyperplastic." The result is difficulty urinating. Hormonal factors play a role, and surgery treats the severe obstructive cases. 6 The common infections of the male tract: the glans and foreskin (nonspecific bacterial, or syphilis, gonorrhea and chlamydia), epididymitis (gonorrhea, chlamydia or a spreading urinary tract infection), and orchitis, which is uncommon (viral, syphilis, tuberculosis, brucellosis) Study guide + recording · 3 questions in the bank Infection of the glans and prepuce (the foreskin) is either nonspecific, such as bacterial, or a specific sexually transmitted disease: syphilis, gonorrhea or chlamydia. Epididymitis: inflammation of the epididymis, from sexually transmitted gonorrhea or chlamydia, or a nonspecific urinary tract infection that spreads to it. Orchitis: inflammation of the testis itself, which is very uncommon: viral, syphilis (Treponema pallidum), tuberculosis, brucellosis and other causes. 7 HPV and the penis, the lecture's "remember": types 6 and 11 cause condyloma acuminatum, benign and verrucous; types 16 and 18 cause penile intraepithelial neoplasia, flat and red, 30 percent invasive if untreated; the HPV-independent kind comes with lichen sclerosus in older men Flagged in the recording · 5 questions in the bank Know this HPV 6 and 11: condyloma acuminatum, benign and verrucous. HPV 16 and 18: penile intraepithelial neoplasia, flat and red, 30 percent invasive if untreated. The HPV-independent kind comes with lichen sclerosus in men over 60. HPV-associated, the more frequent: from the high-risk types, 16 and 18. "So remember, the lower numbers, 6 and 11, are benign. Higher numbers, 16 and 18, are premalignant." HPV-independent: in older men (over 60) with chronic inflammation of the foreskin and glans, an atrophic epithelium and lichen sclerosus; the less frequent kind. Cause HPV 6 and 11 (low risk) HPV 16 and 18 (high risk) No HPV: chronic inflammation, atrophy, lichen sclerosus Behavior Benign, sexually transmitted, contagious Premalignant: 30 percent invasive if untreated Premalignant Who Any age, sexually active The more frequent kind Older men, over 60 Look White, verrucous, exophytic Flat, reddish, may ulcerate Flat, with an atrophic epithelium 8 Phimosis and carcinoma of the penis, the closing review: a foreskin that can't retract fills with smegma, then infection, chronic inflammation and carcinoma; penile squamous cell carcinoma is rare in the United States, tied to poor hygiene, indolent, and spreads to the inguinal nodes Flagged in the recording · 3 questions in the bank Not frequent in the United States, more common in developing countries and in patients of lower socioeconomic status: poor hygiene, phimosis and chronic inflammation of the foreskin predispose to HPV infection and then carcinoma. Its course is indolent: it can spread to the inguinal lymph nodes but not much further. The heaviest burden is the psychological stigma of a tumor of the genitals. 9 Urothelial carcinoma: 90 percent of urinary tract tumors, most in the bladder, in adult men, with minimal painless hematuria; smoking is the strongest risk (four times, and quitting doesn't lower it), with dyes, pelvic radiation, cyclophosphamide and catheters; Schistosoma haematobium causes squamous cell carcinoma Flagged in the recording · 7 questions in the bank Know this Smoking: four times the risk of urothelial carcinoma, and quitting doesn't lower it. The other risks: dyes, rubber, leather and textiles; pelvic radiation for cervical cancer; cyclophosphamide; chronic catheters and infections; Schistosoma haematobium (squamous cell carcinoma, Egypt). Smoking, the strongest: urothelial carcinoma is four times more frequent in smokers, and unlike lung cancer, the risk doesn't go down after quitting. Occupational exposures: work with rubber, leather, textiles and dyes (anilines, beta-naphthylamine) and paints. Schistosoma haematobium, a parasite: a frequent cause of squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder in Africa, especially Egypt ("if you have patients that are coming from Egypt, you can relate"). 10 The two emergencies of the testis: torsion (a twisted spermatic cord infarcts the testis) and inguinal hernia (bowel trapped in an open inguinal canal can infarct) Flagged in the recording · 4 questions in the bank Know this Testicular torsion (a twisted cord, the testis infarcts) and inguinal hernia (bowel trapped in an open inguinal canal, the bowel infarcts) are emergencies. Testicular torsion: a loose spermatic cord twists in the inguinal canal and cuts off the testis's blood supply, which can lead to infarction. Losing one testis won't make a man infertile (there's another), but torsion is a medical emergency. Inguinal hernia: the testes start out retroperitoneal before birth and descend through the inguinal canal, which can still be open in the first years of life. A loop of intestine can slip into the canal and get trapped: sudden pain on one side of the groin, and an emergency, because that segment of bowel can infarct. Also flagged in class 90 percent of urinary tract tumors are urothelial carcinomas, and most are in the bladder; squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma and mesenchymal tumors are the rest. The split to know: seminoma (radiosensitive, behaves very well) versus the non-seminomatous tumors (embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma, teratoma), which don't respond as well. BPH around the urethra (transition zone): it obstructs the urine. Carcinoma in the peripheral zone: it doesn't obstruct early. Prostatic adenocarcinoma, the most frequent cancer in men (over 65): osteoblastic bone metastases; an osteoblastic lesion means a serum PSA. Gleason grades the differentiation, from well-formed glands to masses and single cells; the worse the differentiation, the worse the prognosis. The closing review: cryptorchidism predisposes to testicular cancer; phimosis predisposes to carcinoma of the penis. Skip the WHO classification of urinary tract tumors; know that 90 percent are urothelial carcinomas, mostly in the bladder. Skip the full classification of testicular tumors; sort them into seminoma and non-seminomatous. Skip the seminoma's look under the microscope; know its cut surface (white, solid, no hemorrhage or necrosis) and who gets it. Skip each non-seminomatous tumor's features (embryonal carcinoma's necrosis, the yolk sac tumor's Schiller-Duval bodies, choriocarcinoma's beta-hCG, the teratoma's tissues); know them as the non-seminomatous group, more aggressive and less radiosensitive than seminoma.
